newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: New Zealand's former auditor jailed for fraud.
newsitem.headline: New Zealand's former auditor jailed for fraud.

text.p: New Zealand's former auditor-general, the public sector's top financial watchdog, was jailed for six months on Friday on fraud charges involving more than NZ$60,000 (US$41,820).
Jeff Chapman was sentenced in the Wellington High Court on charges of using a document with intent to defraud.
The charges related to incidents between 1991 and 1994, starting with a memo that Chapman used to seek an advance of NZ$20,000 towards costs of travel to Indonesia.
Some of the charges dated from Chapman's time as head of the state's Accident Compensation Corporation (ACC) before becoming auditor-general in 1992.
The crimes carried a maximum of seven years' imprisonment, but Judge Robert McGechan said there were mitigating circumstances for a reduced sentence.
McGechan noted the offences were not theft, they were not a long-term scheme to create a nest-egg, Chapman was a first offender and he was taking steps to pay it back.
Chapman had also had to suffer public disgrace and would never hold a senior position again, the judge said.
"You have, not to labour the point, fallen a long way and the fall must be a painful one," McGechan said.
Chapman was abroad for nearly three months during his 22 months as auditor-general, taking five separate overseas trips with his wife.
In 1993, Chapman and his wife stayed two days in a NZ$1,100-a-night suite on a taxpayer-funded trip to Monaco, which included helicopter transfers to and from Nice.
But his life fell apart two and a half years ago when he quit his NZ$153,000-a-year position as auditor-general, citing a personal financial situation "incompatible" with his role.
Chapman, 58, had used money from office accounts to cover personal debts resulting from an increasingly chaotic financial situation.
Prosecutors painted a picture at his trial of a man driven by "extravagance, petty greed and dishonesty".
But he maintained his innocence throughout, blaming muddled accounting systems at both ACC and the Audit Office, a disorganised approach to his own finances and a heavy workload.
